workedExamples.stem:
The masses of bags of flour filled by a machine are normally distributed with mean 1500 g and standard deviation 20 g. A bag is picked at random.
Given that its mass is less than 1524 g, find the probability that its mass is less than 1470 g.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

steps.decision: Sketch first: shade less than 1524 lightly and less than 1470 darker. The darker region sits inside the lighter one, so "both" is just the inner event and its probability alone goes on top.

options: Every value less than 1470 is also less than 1524, so "both" is just the first event
The smaller number always goes on top of a fraction
Multiplying the two tails on top would give the same answer
whyMenu.explain: The sheet's formula puts "both" on top. Because the 1470 region lies inside the 1524 region, "both" is the inner event itself. Multiplying the tails would only be right for independent events, and would hand back the smaller tail.

steps.decision: The condition first. 1524 is above the mean, so the region to its left is more than half the curve: the table value itself.
The inner event: 1470 is below the mean, so its left tail is the mirror image of the right tail above +1.5: 1 minus the table value.
Divide, rounding only at the end. A quick check: 0.0755 is bigger than 0.0668 and below 1, as a nested conditional must be.

steps.decision: Sketch first: shade more than 48 lightly and more than 54 darker. The darker region sits inside the lighter one, so "both" is just the inner event and its probability alone goes on top.
The condition first. 48 is below the mean, so everything above it is more than half the curve: by symmetry, the table value itself, with nothing taken from 1.

options: The region above a negative z is the mirror image of the region below +0.8
The table gives the area to the right, so no subtraction is needed
A negative z always means the probability is the table value
whyMenu.explain: Reflect the curve in the mean: the region above z = -0.8 becomes the region below z = 0.8, which is exactly what the table gives. The table always gives the area to the left of a positive z.

steps.decision: The inner event: 54 is above the mean, so the region beyond it is a right-hand tail: 1 minus the table value.
Divide, rounding only at the end. A quick check: 0.0695 is bigger than 0.0548 and below 1, as a nested conditional must be.

workedExamples.stem:
A netball player scores from each shot with probability 0.4, independently. She takes 6 shots.
Given that she scores at least once, find the probability that she scores at least twice.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

steps.decision: Every count in 'at least 2' is also in 'at least 1', so the two events are nested and the smaller one's probability alone goes on top.

options: Every count from 2 to 6 is also a count from 1 to 6
The larger probability always goes on the bottom of any fraction
At least 2 and at least 1 are independent
whyMenu.explain: Nested means one set of outcomes lies inside the other: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 are all among 1 to 6. So 'at least 2 and at least 1' is simply 'at least 2', and nothing is multiplied.

steps.decision: None means every shot misses, so it is q multiplied by itself six times.
Exactly one: the coefficient 6 from row 6 of Pascal's triangle, the one success and the 5 misses.
At least one leaves out only the count 0.
At least two is at least one with the count 1 taken off.
Divide and round once, at the end. Check: 0.8042 is bigger than 0.76672 and below 1.

A basketball player scores each free throw with probability 0.3, independently. She takes 6 free throws.

steps.decision: Exactly two is one of the counts in 'at least one', so the single term goes on top and the condition on the bottom.

options: The count 2 is one of the counts 1 to 6
Exactly two and at least one cannot happen together
whyMenu.explain: If she scores exactly twice she has certainly scored at least once, so 'both' is just 'exactly two'. The bottom is every count from 1 upwards, 1 minus P(0), never P(1) on its own.

steps.decision: The coefficient 15 is from row 6 of Pascal's triangle; the power of p is the number of scores, the power of q the misses.
At least once is everything except scoring none.
Divide and round once. Check: 0.3674 is a little bigger than 0.324135, and below 1.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on earlier work. The probability of no heads in four tosses of a fair coin is 0.0625. What is the probability of at least one head?
items.skill: The complement of 'none' (from the binomial topic)

options.feedback: Yes: at least one head is everything except no heads, so it is $1 - 0.0625$. The same move gives the bottom of most binomial conditionals in this topic.
That is the probability of no heads at all. At least one head is everything else: $1 - 0.0625 = 0.9375$.
That is $4 \times 0.0625$. At least one head is simpler: everything except no heads, $1 - 0.0625 = 0.9375$.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. The Normal Probability Table gives $\Phi(1.2) = 0.8849$. What is $P(Z < -1.2)$?
items.skill: A left tail below a negative z (from the normal-table topic)

options.feedback: Yes: the tail below $-1.2$ is the mirror image of the tail above $+1.2$, so it is $1 - 0.8849$.
That is the area to the left of $+1.2$, more than half the curve. The tail below $-1.2$ is small: $1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151$.
A probability is never negative. The tail below $-1.2$ is the mirror image of the tail above $+1.2$: $1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151$.

items.stem: One more from earlier work. Of 40 pupils, 25 walk to school, and 10 of the walkers live within a mile. A walker is picked at random. What is the probability that she lives within a mile?
items.skill: A conditional probability from counts (from the conditional probability topic)

options.feedback: Yes: 'a walker is picked' makes the 25 walkers the whole, and 10 of them live within a mile.
That divides by every pupil. The pupil picked is a walker, so the whole is the 25 walkers: $\frac{10}{25}$.
That is the probability of being a walker. The question asks, among walkers, for those within a mile: $\frac{10}{25}$.

items.stem: $T$ is normally distributed. What is the probability that both $T < 30$ and $T < 45$ hold?
items.skill: Recognising that 'both' is the inner event of a nested pair

options.feedback: Yes: every value under 30 is also under 45, so 'both' is just $T < 30$.
A product is 'both' only for independent events. Here being under 30 settles being under 45, so 'both' is just $P(T < 30)$.
That is the larger event. 'Both' needs a value under 30 as well, and every such value is already under 45: $P(T < 30)$.

items.stem: Heights $H$ are normally distributed. Which expression gives $P(H > 180 \mid H > 170)$?
items.skill: Setting up the fraction for two 'more than' events

options.feedback: Yes: over 180 is the far tail, inside over 170, so it goes on top alone.
That is upside down and comes out above 1. The condition, over 170, goes on the bottom.
The product on top cancels and hands back $P(H > 180)$. Over 180 is inside over 170, so the top is $P(H > 180)$ alone.

items.stem: In a binomial question, which probability goes on the bottom of $P(X = 2 \mid X \geq 1)$?
items.skill: The condition 'at least one' as 1 minus P(0)

options.feedback: Yes: at least one is every count except 0.
That is exactly one. At least one also counts 2, 3 and upwards: $1 - P(0)$.
That is at least two: it leaves out the count 1, which 'at least one' includes. The bottom is $1 - P(0)$.

items.stem: Event $A$ lies inside event $B$, with $P(A) = 0.2$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(A \mid B)$?
items.skill: The nested rule and the size check

options.feedback: Yes: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$, bigger than 0.2 and below 1, as a nested conditional must be.
That is $0.2 \times 0.5$, which would be 'both' for independent events. A conditional divides: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$.
Above 1, so the fraction is upside down. The condition goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$.
That is $P(A)$ itself, as if the condition changed nothing. Given $B$, the whole shrinks to $B$: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$.

items.stem: In a binomial question, which fraction gives $P(X = 3 \mid X \geq 2)$?
items.skill: A condition other than 'at least one'

options.feedback: Yes: at least two leaves out the counts 0 and 1, and the count 3 sits inside it.
That bottom is at least one. The condition is at least two, so the count 1 must come off as well.
That reads 'at least two' as 'exactly two'. At least two is every count from 2 upwards: $1 - P(0) - P(1)$.

items.stem: Lengths $L$ are normal with mean 240 cm and standard deviation 4 cm. For $L > 236$, $z = -1$. Which is $P(L > 236)$?
items.skill: The region above a negative z, the condition of a 'more than' pair

options.feedback: Yes: the region above $-1$ is the mirror image of the region below $+1$, which the table gives directly.
That is the small tail, under a half; but most lengths are above 236 cm, which is below the mean. By symmetry the answer is $\Phi(1)$.
That is only the band from 236 cm up to the mean. Every length above the mean counts too, so the region is everything above $z = -1$: $\Phi(1)$.

context.setting: Swimming badges held by the members of a club

parts.stem:
At a swimming club, 75% of the members hold a distance badge and 30% hold a gold badge. Every gold badge holder also holds a distance badge.
A member who holds a distance badge is picked at random. Find the probability that she also holds a gold badge.
hints: Every gold badge holder is inside the distance-badge group, so the two events are nested.
The share of the distance-badge group that holds gold: gold over distance.
parts.workedSolution:
Gold sits inside distance, so "gold and distance" is just gold.
$P(\text{gold} \mid \text{distance}) = \frac{0.3}{0.75}$
$= 0.4$

commonErrors.feedback: 0.3 is the gold probability handed back: either nothing was divided, or the top was $0.3 \times 0.75$ and the bottom 0.75, which cancel. The whole is now the distance-badge group, so divide: $\frac{0.3}{0.75} = 0.4$.

0.225 is $0.3 \times 0.75$, which would be "both" for independent events. Gold badge holders all hold distance badges, so "both" is just gold, and the answer divides by the condition: $\frac{0.3}{0.75} = 0.4$.
2.5 is more than 1, so the fraction is upside down. The condition, the distance badge, goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.3}{0.75} = 0.4$.

context.setting: Wins in five turns of a fairground game

parts.stem:
Aoife has five turns at a fairground game. The probability that she wins at least once is 0.7, and the probability that she wins at least twice is 0.35.

$P(\text{at least 2} \mid \text{at least 1}) = \frac{0.35}{0.7}$
$= 0.5$

0.245 is $0.35 \times 0.7$. The two events are nested, not independent, and a conditional divides: $\frac{0.35}{0.7} = 0.5$.
2 is more than 1: the fraction is upside down. The condition, at least one win, goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.35}{0.7} = 0.5$.

context.setting: Scores in a national reading test

parts.stem:
Scores in a national reading test are normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 10. One pupil's score, $S$, is picked at random. From the table, $P(S < 71) = 0.9821$.
Find the probability that the score is less than 58.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Work out z first: the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation.
Everything to the left of a positive z is the table value itself.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.2119 is the area to the RIGHT of $z = 0.8$. Everything below 58, to the left of a positive $z$, is more than half the curve: it is the table value itself, 0.7881.

parts.stem:
Given that the score is less than 71, find the probability that it is less than 58.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Is every value less than 58 also less than 71?
Then the smaller event's probability alone goes on top, and the condition's on the bottom.
parts.workedSolution:
Every value less than 58 is also less than 71, so the two events are nested.
$P(S < 58 \mid S < 71) = \frac{P(S < 58)}{P(S < 71)}$
$= \frac{0.7881}{0.9821}$
$= 0.8025$

commonErrors.feedback: 0.7881 is the smaller probability handed back unchanged: the top was taken as 0.7881 × 0.9821 and then divided by 0.9821. Every value less than 58 is already less than 71, so "both" is just the first event: $\frac{0.7881}{0.9821} = 0.8025$.

0.7740 is the two probabilities multiplied, which would answer "both" for independent events. These two are nested, and a conditional divides: the smaller event's probability over the condition's, $\frac{0.7881}{0.9821} = 0.8025$.
1.2462 is more than 1, so it cannot be a probability: the fraction is upside down. The condition's probability goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.7881}{0.9821} = 0.8025$.

parts.stem:
Each parcel sent by a courier is damaged with probability 0.15, independently of the others. Maeve sends 7 parcels. $X$ is the number damaged.
Find the probability that none of the parcels is damaged.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.6794 is $1 - 0.85^{7}$, the probability of at least one damaged parcel. None is the single term with every trial a failure: $0.85^{7} = 0.3206$, with nothing taken from 1.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.2097 is $P(X = 2)$ alone. "At least 2" is 2 or more: every count from 2 to 7. The quick way is 1 minus the counts left out: $1 - (P(0) + P(1)) = 0.2834$.
0.6794 takes away $P(0)$ only. For at least 2, every count below 2 is left out: $1 - (P(0) + P(1)) = 0.2834$.

The times, $T$ minutes, taken to charge a laptop battery fully are normally distributed with mean 64 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes.
Find the probability that a battery picked at random takes less than 76 minutes to charge.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Work out z first: the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation.
Everything to the left of a positive z is the table value itself.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.0228 is the area to the RIGHT of $z = 2$. Everything below 76, to the left of a positive $z$, is more than half the curve: it is the table value itself, 0.9772.

parts.stem:
Find the probability that a battery picked at random takes less than 55 minutes to charge.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Work out z first: the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation.
A left tail below a negative z is the mirror image of the right tail above the positive z: 1 minus the table value.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.9332 is the area to the left of $+1.5$. The region wanted is below $-1.5$, the mirror image of the tail above $+1.5$, so it is what is left of 1: $1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668$. A sketch with both values marked shows it at once.

parts.stem:
Find the probability that a battery takes less than 55 minutes to charge, given that it takes less than 76 minutes.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Is every value less than 55 also less than 76?
Then the smaller event's probability alone goes on top, and the condition's on the bottom.
parts.workedSolution:
Every value less than 55 is also less than 76, so the two events are nested.
$P(T < 55 \mid T < 76) = \frac{P(T < 55)}{P(T < 76)}$
$= \frac{0.0668}{0.9772}$
$= 0.0684$

commonErrors.feedback: 0.0668 is the smaller probability handed back unchanged: the top was taken as 0.0668 × 0.9772 and then divided by 0.9772. Every value less than 55 is already less than 76, so "both" is just the first event: $\frac{0.0668}{0.9772} = 0.0684$.

0.0653 is the two probabilities multiplied, which would answer "both" for independent events. These two are nested, and a conditional divides: the smaller event's probability over the condition's, $\frac{0.0668}{0.9772} = 0.0684$.
14.6287 is more than 1, so it cannot be a probability: the fraction is upside down. The condition's probability goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.0668}{0.9772} = 0.0684$.

context.setting: Reds on a spinner

parts.stem:
A spinner lands on red with probability 0.25 on each spin, independently. It is spun 7 times. $X$ is the number of reds.
Find the probability that the spinner never lands on red.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: None means every one of the 7 trials is a failure.
So it is $q$ multiplied by itself 7 times.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.8665 is $1 - 0.75^{7}$, the probability of at least one red. None is the single term with every trial a failure: $0.75^{7} = 0.1335$, with nothing taken from 1.

parts.stem:
Find the probability that the spinner lands on red at least three times.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: At least 3 leaves out only the counts below 3.
Find P(0) + P(1) + P(2), then take the total from 1.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.1730 is $P(X = 3)$ alone. "At least 3" is 3 or more: every count from 3 to 7. The quick way is 1 minus the counts left out: $1 - (P(0) + P(1) + P(2)) = 0.2436$.
0.5551 takes away $P(0)$ and $P(1)$ only. For at least 3, every count below 3 is left out: $1 - (P(0) + P(1) + P(2)) = 0.2436$.
0.9871 uses $p$ and $q$ the wrong way round. The success here has probability 0.25, so each term is a power of 0.25 times a power of 0.75: that gives 0.2436.

parts.stem:
Given that the spinner lands on red at least once, find the probability that it lands on red at least three times.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

scheme.for: $1 - 0.1335$, the probability of at least one

hints: Every count in "at least 3" is also in "at least 1".
So the smaller event's probability alone goes on top, and the condition's on the bottom.
parts.workedSolution:
Every count in "at least 3" is also in "at least 1", so the events are nested.
$P(X \geq 1) = 1 - 0.1335$
$= 0.8665$
$P(X \geq 3 \mid X \geq 1) = \frac{0.2436}{0.8665}$
$= 0.2811$

commonErrors.feedback: 0.2436 is the top of the fraction on its own. Given the condition, the answer is a share of the condition's probability: divide, $\frac{0.2436}{0.8665} = 0.2811$.

0.2111 is the two probabilities multiplied, which would answer "both" for independent events. These two are nested, and a conditional divides: the smaller event's probability over the condition's, $\frac{0.2436}{0.8665} = 0.2811$.
3.5573 is more than 1, so it cannot be a probability: the fraction is upside down. The condition's probability goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.2436}{0.8665} = 0.2811$.
0.7821 divides by $P(X = 1)$ alone. "Given at least one" makes every count from 1 upwards the whole, so the bottom is $1 - P(0) = 0.8665$, and $\frac{0.2436}{0.8665} = 0.2811$.

context.setting: Burning times of candles

parts.stem:
The burning times, $T$ hours, of a brand of candle are normally distributed with mean 30 hours and standard deviation 3 hours.
Find the probability that a candle picked at random burns for more than 27 hours 36 minutes.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Work out z first: the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation.
The region above a negative z is more than half the curve: by symmetry it is the table value for the size of z.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.2119 is under a half, but most values lie above 27.6, which is below the mean. By symmetry the region above $z = -0.8$ is the table value for 0.8: 0.7881, with nothing taken from 1.

parts.stem:
Find the probability that a candle picked at random burns for more than 34 hours 12 minutes.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Work out z first: the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation.
The table gives the area to the left of z; the right tail is what is left of 1.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.9192 is the area to the LEFT of $z = 1.4$, which is what the table always gives. The region above 34.2 is the right-hand tail, what is left of 1: $1 - 0.9192 = 0.0808$.

parts.stem:
Given that a candle burns for more than 27 hours 36 minutes, find the probability that it burns for more than 34 hours 12 minutes.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
hints: Is every value more than 34.2 also more than 27.6?
Then the smaller event's probability alone goes on top, and the condition's on the bottom.
parts.workedSolution:
Every value more than 34.2 is also more than 27.6, so the two events are nested.
$P(T > 34.2 \mid T > 27.6) = \frac{P(T > 34.2)}{P(T > 27.6)}$
$= \frac{0.0808}{0.7881}$
$= 0.1025$

commonErrors.feedback: 0.0808 is the smaller probability handed back unchanged: the top was taken as 0.0808 × 0.7881 and then divided by 0.7881. Every value more than 34.2 is already more than 27.6, so "both" is just the first event: $\frac{0.0808}{0.7881} = 0.1025$.

0.0637 is the two probabilities multiplied, which would answer "both" for independent events. These two are nested, and a conditional divides: the smaller event's probability over the condition's, $\frac{0.0808}{0.7881} = 0.1025$.
9.7537 is more than 1, so it cannot be a probability: the fraction is upside down. The condition's probability goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.0808}{0.7881} = 0.1025$.

findTheMistake.stem: Ferry crossing times are normally distributed with mean 44 minutes and standard deviation 3 minutes. Niamh was asked for $P(T < 39.2 \mid T < 47.6)$ to 4 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 multiplies the two tails on top. Every time under 39.2 minutes is also under 47.6, so "both" is just $T < 39.2$: the top is 0.0548 alone. As written, the product cancels with the bottom and hands back 0.0548.
findTheMistake.feedback: Both tails are right, and in the paper they would earn their own parts' marks. The 2 marks for the conditional go at line 3. A check would have caught it: an answer equal to the smaller tail means the condition changed nothing, and a nested condition always makes the probability bigger.

findTheMistake.stem: Each of 7 raffle tickets wins a prize with probability 0.2, independently. Callum was asked for the probability that at least two tickets win, given that at least one does, to 4 decimal places. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 5 gives the top of the fraction as the answer. He found both pieces, P(at least 2) and P(at least 1), but never divided one by the other. Given at least one win, the answer is a share of that condition: 0.4233 ÷ 0.7903.
findTheMistake.feedback: Every line up to line 4 is right: the complement for at least one, and at least two from it. The method mark for finding the condition's probability is safe; the fraction and its value are what line 5 leaves out.

findTheMistake.stem: The masses of newborn lambs on a farm are normally distributed with mean 3.5 kg and standard deviation 0.4 kg. Orla was asked for $P(M > 4.18 \mid M > 3.06)$ to 4 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 takes the table value from 1. 3.06 kg is below the mean, so most lambs weigh more than it: the region above $z = -1.1$ is more than half the curve and, by symmetry, is the table value itself, 0.8643.
findTheMistake.feedback: Her z-values are right and her fraction is set up the right way round, so those marks are safe. The region went wrong at line 1, and the answer, 0.3287, is far too big as a result. A sketch with 3.06 kg left of the mean shows the region above it is most of the curve.

prompts.prompt: Event A lies inside event B. What is P(A | B)?
prompts.answer: P(A) divided by P(B): because A is inside B, 'A and B' is just A.

prompts.prompt: Why must P(T < 34) not be multiplied by P(T < 60) on the top of the fraction?
prompts.answer: Multiplying gives 'both' only for independent events. Under 34 lies inside under 60, so 'both' is just P(T < 34).

prompts.prompt: What is the quick size check on a nested conditional probability?
prompts.answer: It is at least the smaller event's own probability and never above 1; above 1 means the fraction is upside down.

prompts.prompt: The normal question ends with a 2-mark 'given that' part. What are the two marks for?
prompts.answer: The first for the fraction, part (ii)'s tail over part (i)'s; the second for its value to 4 decimal places.

prompts.prompt: For n binomial trials, how do you find P(X ≥ 1)?
prompts.answer: 1 minus P(0), which is 1 minus q to the power n.

prompts.prompt: Given at least one success, what goes on top for 'exactly r successes'?
prompts.answer: The single term P(X = r) from the expansion; the bottom is 1 minus P(0).

prompts.prompt: A condition says a battery 'does not last more than 30 hours'. Which region is it?
prompts.answer: The left tail, T < 30: turn the words into an inequality before any arithmetic.

prompts.prompt: Both events say 'more than'. Which tail goes on top?
prompts.answer: The far tail, beyond the larger value: it lies inside the near tail, which goes on the bottom.

prompts.prompt: In a chain from the normal into the binomial, what becomes p?
prompts.answer: The normal tail for one trial, read from the table: the chance that a single item meets the condition.

prompts.prompt: Where does this specification stop for conditionals through a distribution?
prompts.answer: Every one is nested; a pair needing the area between two values, or a value found from a probability, is not set.

findings.asked: Less than 34 given less than 60, from two normal tails.
findings.wentWrong: Most multiplied the two probabilities on the top, not seeing that under 34 lies inside under 60.
findings.rule: If one event lies inside the other, its probability alone goes on top: divide, never multiply.

findings.asked: Less than 36 given less than 50, from two normal tails.
findings.wentWrong: Only the top 40% scored; the product on the top gave back 0.1151, the smaller tail.
findings.rule: An answer equal to the smaller tail means the condition changed nothing: divide by the condition's tail.

findings.asked: Three beads the same colour, given the first two the same.
findings.wentWrong: Under a third scored; most did not see that three the same already includes two the same.
findings.rule: Nested on a tree: the smaller event's branch total alone goes on top.

findings.asked: A conditional from a three-set Venn diagram, given not in one set.
findings.wentWrong: The numerator was usually right; the denominator was not.
findings.rule: The bottom is the condition's own group, counted first.

findings.asked: The first set won, given the second set won, from a tree.
findings.wentWrong: Many found the top or the bottom; only the best combined them.
findings.rule: Find both pieces, then divide one by the other.

insight.ruleToRemember: Sketch both regions; if one lies inside the other, the smaller probability alone goes on top. Divide, never multiply, and check the answer is below 1.
insight.aStarSignal: The full-mark answers wrote the fraction before any value: the smaller event's probability over the condition's.
